meta.title: Digital Exhibition — WordPress & App Recap
meta.subtitle: Where the WordPress site and the new Nuxt application stand, what we are waiting for, and how the pieces fit together
meta.client: TU/e — Built Environment, Digital Exhibition platform
meta.author: marco@tech-paw.com
meta.scope: Staging / local only for now — nothing described here has been pushed to the live server.

tldr: The live WordPress site is unchanged apart from a few plugins added or removed. All the new work sits on staging / localhost.

The new front-end is a Nuxt application on Cloudflare. It reads pages from the WordPress REST API and shows them in a new layout, so WordPress stays the place where editors work. We still need to decide where the web app (Nuxt) is going to live.
Images come from one shared bucket for live, staging and the app (16.5 GB), instead of three copies.

Before we go live we need: a decision on hosting (Cloudflare or somewhere else), approval of staging, confirmation of the SEO set-up, an email service, and testing of desktop, mobile and forms (most of these parts have already been tested).

actions.title: Email system
actions.detail: Password reset and the contact form need a working mail service. Brevo is the proposed option (free plan: 300 emails per day) as an alternative to Microsoft Graph via Azure. WP Mail SMTP on WordPress and the contact endpoint in the app both connect to it.
actions.ask: Choose Brevo or Microsoft Graph, so the sender domain can be set up.

actions.title: SEO optimisation
actions.detail: On WordPress, SEO is handled by Yoast and the data is essential. In the app SEO is more complete and many pages carry sensible defaults. Indexing stays switched off until go-live.
actions.ask: Confirm the app's SEO approach is acceptable.

actions.title: Approve the staging website
actions.detail: Two databases exist, staging and production. They are not synchronised, but both are up to date. Staging holds the new admin experience.
actions.ask: Log in to the new back end, review it and confirm, so the final transfer can start.

actions.title: Decide the hosting
actions.detail: Where the web application (Nuxt on Cloudflare) and the bucket (R2?) will live. Jonathan suggests Bunny.net.
actions.ask: Decide the hosting for the app and the bucket.

actions.title: Merge staging and turn it into production
actions.detail: The live site has barely changed (a few plugins added or removed). Once both repositories are merged, live becomes a copy of staging and the database is adapted, with a few changes made either on staging or through code.

actions.title: Tests before going live
actions.detail: Most parts have already been tested. Before the domain is transferred, the application gets a final check on desktop and mobile, including the forms. On WordPress, the new admin UX/UI gets manual and automated testing.
actions.ask: Manual and automated testing of the new WordPress interface.

actions.title: Plugins and Flask
actions.detail: We need to know whether Flask has any connection to WordPress through the various plugins.
actions.ask: Confirm whether any plugin depends on a connection with Flask.

plugins.name: Figuro Folders
plugins.does: Media library folders. It replaces FileBird Pro; the folders and files were imported from FileBird (438 folders, 3,943 files in the latest import).

plugins.name: SVG Support
plugins.does: Allows SVG uploads such as logos and other vector images.

plugins.name: Advanced Media Offloader
plugins.does: Sends uploads to the Cloudflare R2 bucket so live, staging and the app share one copy of every image.

plugins.name: Activity Log
plugins.does: Records who changed what in the WordPress admin.

plugins.name: WP Mail SMTP
plugins.does: Will be connected to the email service, so password resets and form mails are delivered.

plugins.name: Cloudflare Deploy Trigger
plugins.does: A “Deploy Frontend” button. Editors write their pages, then press it once to publish them in the app. This saves API calls and avoids extra cost.

environments.title: Test new features
environments.text: Try changes on the WordPress site before they reach the live site.

environments.title: Emergency replica
environments.text: If something goes wrong, staging can copy the live environment to reproduce and find errors.

email.title: Brevo as the email service
email.text: Brevo is an alternative to Microsoft Graph via Azure. Its free plan allows 300 emails per day, which is enough for password resets and the contact form.

postmortem.title: Post-mortem — the theme update that broke the front-end
postmortem.summary: Automatic updates on the Flask server updated the WordPress theme. Because the theme had no child theme, the update replaced it completely with the files from the WordPress repository, which broke the theme and the WordPress front-end design.

chain.label: Automatic update
chain.text: Flask runs automatic updates for WordPress.

chain.label: Theme updated
chain.text: The theme was set up without a child theme, so it updates as a whole.

chain.label: Files overwritten
chain.text: The update downloads the files from the WordPress repository over the customised ones.

chain.label: Front-end broken
chain.text: The theme and the WordPress front-end design stop working.

now.title: Where we are now

points.text: Switching auto-update off in WordPress was not enough: the theme still updated.
On the live site we changed the theme name, to avoid the auto-update.
The theme is maintained as it was in the previous version. Only its name changed, so the design and files stay the same.

now.question: Was auto-update switched off only after the update had already happened? TU/e IT can confirm the order of events.
